pattern.top_pattern: Rare high-cost inpatient outliers need case-level review, not broad policy changes
pattern.what_is_impacting: CA, CT, NH, OH, and GA rare inpatient outliers

providers: ST. JOSEPH'S HOSPITAL AND MEDICAL CENTER

key_driver_codes: Tracheostomy with Mechanical Ventilation >96 Hours or Principal Diagnosis Except Face, Mouth and Neck without Major O.R. Procedures
Septicemia or Severe Sepsis without Mechanical Ventilation >96 Hours with MCC
Respiratory Infections and Inflammations with MCC
pattern.pattern_details: A separate set of rare, very expensive inpatient cases is appearing across CA, CT, NH, OH, and GA. These include tracheostomy with prolonged ventilation, lung transplant complications, transplant aftercare, severe trauma, sepsis, pneumonia, and respiratory infection cases, usually as one-off admissions. They are too episodic to support broad policy changes, but they do warrant catastrophic case management, coding confirmation, and individual payment review.
pattern.why_it_matters: A small number of catastrophic or unusual cases can materially affect results and should be managed at the case level.
pattern.recommended_next_step: Route these cases to clinical and data-quality review to confirm coding, episode classification, and case management capture, and use individual payment review rather than changing broad utilization policy.
pattern.validation_reason: The pattern is driven by one-off or very small-count admissions with repeated low-baseline flags, so case-level confirmation is needed before any broader interpretation.
evidence_summary: Multi-state rare high-cost cases added about $687K, including a tracheostomy and lung transplant complication admission at about $152K and a severe trauma case at about $73K.
GA and OH rare aftercare outliers added about $130K, including lung transplant aftercare and traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage episodes.
Multi-state sepsis, pneumonia, and respiratory infection one-off admissions added about $100K combined.
